verses.t: Gongsun Chou asked, "Master, if you were to hold power in Qi, could the achievements of Guan Zhong and Yanzi be expected again?" Mencius said, "You are truly a man of Qi: you know only Guan Zhong and Yanzi. Someone once asked Zeng Xi, 'Who is more worthy, you or Zilu?' Zeng Xi said uneasily, 'He was one whom my late grandfather held in awe.' 'Then who is more worthy, you or Guan Zhong?' Zeng Xi flushed with displeasure and said, 'How can you compare me with Guan Zhong? Guan Zhong had his ruler's confidence so completely, and directed the government of the state for so long, and yet his achievements were so mean. How can you compare me with such a man?'" Mencius went on, "Guan Zhong was someone Zeng Xi would not wish to be. Do you wish it for me?" Gongsun Chou said, "Guan Zhong made his ruler leader of the feudal lords, and Yanzi made his ruler illustrious. Are Guan Zhong and Yanzi still not worth emulating?" Mencius said, "To make Qi a true kingship would be as easy as turning over one's hand." "If that is so, my perplexity is all the greater. With all the virtue of King Wen, who lived to be a hundred before he died, his influence still did not spread over the whole world; only when King Wu and the Duke of Zhou carried on his work did it prevail everywhere. Now you speak as if becoming a true king were easy. Is King Wen then not worth taking as a model?" Mencius said, "How can anyone match King Wen? From Tang down to Wu Ding there arose six or seven worthy and sage rulers. The world had long given its allegiance to Yin, and what has lasted long is hard to change. Wu Ding received the feudal lords at his court and held the whole world as if he were turning it in his palm. Zhou [the tyrant] was not far removed in time from Wu Ding; the old families, the inherited customs, the lingering influences and the good ways of government still survived in part. There were also the Viscount of Wei, Wei Zhong, Prince Bigan, the Viscount of Ji and Jiao Ge, all worthy men, who together assisted him. That is why it took a long time before he lost the realm. There was not a foot of land that was not his, not a single person who was not his subject; and King Wen rose from only a hundred li square. That is why it was difficult. The people of Qi have a saying: 'Wisdom and cleverness are not as good as taking advantage of the situation; a good hoe is not as good as waiting for the season.' At the present time it would be easy. In the flourishing days of the Xia, Yin and Zhou, no royal domain exceeded a thousand li, and Qi has that much territory. The crowing of cocks and the barking of dogs can be heard from one place to the next all the way to its four borders, and Qi has that many people. It needs no further land opened up and no further people gathered. If it practises humane government and becomes a true king, no one will be able to stop it. Moreover, never has a true king been longer in arising than now; never have the people suffered more under tyrannical government than now. It is easy to feed the hungry and easy to give drink to the thirsty. Confucius said, 'Virtue spreads faster than a royal order carried by relay stations.' At the present time, if a state of ten thousand chariots practises humane government, the people will rejoice in it as if they had been cut down from hanging upside down. So with half the effort of the ancients, twice the result can be achieved. Only at this time is that so."

Gongsun Chou asked, "Master, suppose you were made a high minister of Qi and could put your Way into practice. Even if this made the ruler a leading lord or a true king, it would be no wonder. In such a position, would your mind be stirred?" Mencius said, "No. At forty my mind ceased to be stirred." "In that case you far surpass Meng Ben." "That is not difficult. Gaozi achieved an unstirred mind before I did." "Is there a way to an unstirred mind?" "There is. Beigong You cultivated his courage like this: he would not flinch when his skin was pierced, nor blink when something was thrust at his eyes. He felt the least slight from anyone as if he had been flogged in the marketplace. He would not take an insult from a coarse-clad commoner, nor would he take one from a ruler of ten thousand chariots. He regarded stabbing the ruler of ten thousand chariots as no different from stabbing a coarse-clad fellow. He held no feudal lord in awe, and whenever an insult came to him he returned it. Mengshi She cultivated his courage like this. He said, 'I regard defeat as if it were victory. To size up the enemy before advancing and weigh the chances of victory before engaging is to be afraid of the opposing armies. How can I be sure of victory? I can only be without fear.' Mengshi She was like Zengzi; Beigong You was like Zixia. Of the courage of these two I do not know which was the more worthy, but Mengshi She held to what was essential. Long ago Zengzi said to Zixiang, 'Do you love courage? I once heard about great courage from the Master [Confucius]: If, on looking within, I find that I am not upright, then even before a coarse-clad commoner I shall be afraid. If, on looking within, I find that I am upright, then even against thousands and tens of thousands I shall go forward.' Yet Mengshi She's holding to his vital energy was still not as good as Zengzi's holding to what is essential." "May I ask you about your unstirred mind, Master, and Gaozi's unstirred mind?" "Gaozi says, 'What you do not grasp in words, do not seek in the mind; what you do not grasp in the mind, do not seek in the vital energy.' 'What you do not grasp in the mind, do not seek in the vital energy' is acceptable; 'what you do not grasp in words, do not seek in the mind' is not. The will is the commander of the vital energy; the vital energy is what fills the body. Where the will goes, the vital energy follows. So it is said: 'Hold fast to your will, and do not abuse your vital energy.'" "You have said, 'Where the will goes, the vital energy follows,' and you also say, 'Hold fast to your will and do not abuse your vital energy.' Why is that?" "When the will is concentrated, it moves the vital energy; when the vital energy is concentrated, it moves the will. Now stumbling and hurrying are matters of the vital energy, yet they in turn stir the mind." "May I ask, Master, in what you excel?" "I understand words, and I am good at nourishing my flood-like vital energy." "May I ask what you mean by flood-like vital energy?" "It is hard to describe. As a vital energy it is supremely great and supremely firm. If it is nourished by uprightness and not harmed, it fills the space between Heaven and Earth. As a vital energy, it is the partner of righteousness and the Way; without these it starves. It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds; it is not something seized by a single righteous act. If one does anything that one's heart is not content with, it starves. That is why I say Gaozi has never understood righteousness, because he regards it as external. You must work at it, but not with a fixed expectation of results. The heart must not forget it, but you must not help it grow. Do not be like the man of Song. There was a man of Song who was worried that his sprouts were not growing, and so he pulled at them. He came home exhausted and said to his family, 'I am worn out today. I have been helping the sprouts to grow.' His son hurried out to look, and the sprouts had withered. There are few in the world who do not help their sprouts to grow. Those who think it useless and leave them alone are those who do not weed their sprouts; those who help them grow are those who pull at their sprouts. This is not merely useless; it does harm." "What do you mean by understanding words?" "When words are one-sided, I know what is hiding [the truth]; when words are extravagant, I know where the speaker has fallen into a trap; when words are deviant, I know where he has departed [from the right]; when words are evasive, I know where he is at a loss. Such things, arising in the mind, do harm to government; and arising in government, do harm to affairs. If a sage arose again, he would surely agree with what I say." [Gongsun Chou said,] "Zai Wo and Zigong were good at speaking; Ran Niu, Minzi and Yan Yuan were good at speaking of virtuous conduct. Confucius had both, yet he said, 'In matters of speech I am not capable.' Then, Master, are you already a sage?" Mencius said, "Oh! What kind of thing is that to say? Long ago Zigong asked Confucius, 'Master, are you a sage?' Confucius said, 'A sage I cannot be. I learn without tiring and teach without wearying.' Zigong said, 'To learn without tiring is wisdom; to teach without wearying is humaneness. Humane and wise: Master, you are already a sage!' Even Confucius would not claim to be a sage. What kind of thing is that to say?" "I once heard that Zixia, Ziyou and Zizhang each had one part of a sage, while Ran Niu, Minzi and Yan Yuan had all the parts, but on a small scale. May I ask with which of these you would be content?" Mencius said, "Let us leave that aside for now." "What about Boyi and Yi Yin?" "Their ways were different. Not to serve a ruler who was not his ruler, not to command people who were not his people; to take office when there was order and withdraw when there was disorder: that was Boyi. Whom may I not serve as my ruler? Whom may I not command as my people? To take office when there was order and also when there was disorder: that was Yi Yin. To take office when it was right to take office, to stop when it was right to stop, to stay long when it was right to stay long, to leave quickly when it was right to leave quickly: that was Confucius. All of them were sages of antiquity. I have not been able to act as any of them did; but what I wish is to learn from Confucius." "Are Boyi and Yi Yin then of the same rank as Confucius?" "No. Since humankind was born there has never been another Confucius." "Then did they have anything in common?" "They did. If any of them had been given a territory of a hundred li to rule, he could have brought the feudal lords to his court and possessed the whole world. And none of them would have committed one unrighteous act or killed one innocent person to gain the world. In this they were alike." "May I ask how they differed?" "Zai Wo, Zigong and You Ruo had wisdom enough to understand a sage, and even at their lowest they would not have flattered the one they loved. Zai Wo said, 'As I see it, the Master far surpassed Yao and Shun.' Zigong said, 'By seeing a ruler's rituals one knows his government; by hearing his music one knows his virtue. Looking back from a hundred generations later and ranking the kings of a hundred generations, none can escape [the Master's judgment]. Since humankind was born there has never been anyone like the Master.' You Ruo said, 'Is it only among people? The qilin among running beasts, the phoenix among flying birds, Mount Tai among hills and mounds, the Yellow River and the sea among roadside puddles: these are of the same kind. The sage among the people is also of the same kind. He stands out from his kind and rises above the crowd, but since humankind was born there has never been one more abundant [in virtue] than Confucius.'"

Mencius said, "One who uses force while borrowing the name of humaneness becomes a leading lord, and a leading lord must have a large state. One who practises humaneness through virtue becomes a true king, and a true king does not depend on size: Tang did it with seventy li, and King Wen with a hundred. When people are subdued by force, they do not submit in their hearts; they submit only because their strength is insufficient. When people are won over by virtue, they are glad in their hearts and sincerely submit, as the seventy disciples submitted to Confucius. The Book of Odes says: 'From the west, from the east, from the south, from the north, there was no thought of not submitting.' This is what it means."

Mencius said, "Humaneness brings honor; lack of humaneness brings disgrace. To hate disgrace and yet remain without humaneness is like hating damp and yet living in a low place. If a ruler hates disgrace, nothing is better than to value virtue and honor scholars, so that the worthy hold positions and the able hold offices. When the state is at peace, he should take that time to make clear his government and laws; then even a great state will be sure to stand in awe of him. The Book of Odes says: 'Before the sky grew dark with rain, I gathered the bark from the mulberry roots and bound fast my window and door. Now, you people below, who will dare to insult me?' Confucius said, 'Whoever made this poem understood the Way! If a ruler can govern his state well, who will dare to insult him?' But now, when the state is at peace, rulers take that time to indulge in pleasure, idleness and arrogance. They are seeking calamity for themselves. Calamity and good fortune are always of our own seeking. The Book of Odes says: 'Ever strive to accord with the mandate, and you will seek out much good fortune for yourself.' The Taijia says: 'Calamities sent by Heaven may still be escaped; calamities one brings on oneself cannot be survived.' This is what it means."

Mencius said, "If a ruler honors the worthy and employs the able, so that outstanding men hold office, then all the scholars of the world will be pleased and wish to stand in his court. If in the market he charges ground-rent on shops but does not tax the goods, or enforces the regulations but does not charge ground-rent, then all the merchants of the world will be pleased and wish to store their goods in his market. If at the frontier passes there is inspection but no tax, then all the travelers of the world will be pleased and wish to journey on his roads. If farmers help to till the public field and pay no other tax, then all the farmers of the world will be pleased and wish to plow in his fields. If there are no levies on dwellings in place of labor service or cloth, then all the people of the world will be pleased and wish to become his subjects. If a ruler can truly practise these five things, the people of neighboring states will look up to him as to father and mother. Since humankind was born, no one has ever succeeded in leading children to attack their own father and mother. Such a ruler will have no enemy in the world, and one who has no enemy in the world is the agent of Heaven. That such a one should fail to become a true king has never happened."

Mencius said, "All people have a heart that cannot bear [to see the suffering of] others. The former kings had a heart that could not bear [the suffering of] others, and so they had a government that could not bear [the suffering of] others. With a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others, practising a government that cannot bear the suffering of others, one could govern the world as easily as turning something in the palm of one's hand. Why do I say that all people have a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others? Suppose people suddenly see a small child about to fall into a well: every one of them will feel alarm and compassion. This is not because they want to win the favor of the child's parents, nor because they want praise from their neighbors and friends, nor because they dislike the sound of [the child's] crying. From this we can see that whoever lacks a heart of compassion is not human; whoever lacks a heart of shame is not human; whoever lacks a heart of deference is not human; whoever lacks a heart of right and wrong is not human. The heart of compassion is the sprout of humaneness; the heart of shame is the sprout of righteousness; the heart of deference is the sprout of ritual propriety; the heart of right and wrong is the sprout of wisdom. People have these four sprouts just as they have four limbs. To have these four sprouts and yet say that one is incapable [of goodness] is to rob oneself; to say that one's ruler is incapable is to rob one's ruler. All who have these four sprouts within themselves, if they know how to extend and fill them out, will be like a fire beginning to burn or a spring beginning to flow. If one can fill them out, they are enough to protect all within the four seas; if one does not fill them out, they are not enough even to serve one's parents."

Mencius said, "Is the arrow-maker less humane than the armor-maker? The arrow-maker's only fear is that his arrows will not wound people; the armor-maker's only fear is that people will be wounded. It is the same with the healer-priest and the coffin-maker. So one must be careful in choosing one's trade. Confucius said, 'It is humaneness that makes a neighborhood beautiful. If one chooses not to dwell in humaneness, how can one be called wise?' Humaneness is the most honorable rank conferred by Heaven and the peaceful home of humankind. To be without humaneness when no one is stopping you is to be unwise. One who is without humaneness, without wisdom, without ritual propriety and without righteousness is a servant of others. To be a servant and be ashamed of serving is like a bow-maker being ashamed of making bows, or an arrow-maker being ashamed of making arrows. If one is ashamed of it, nothing is better than to practise humaneness. Humaneness is like archery: the archer corrects himself and then shoots. If he shoots and misses, he does not resent those who beat him; he simply turns back and looks for the cause in himself."

Mencius said, "When anyone told Zilu that he had a fault, he was glad. When Yu heard good words, he bowed. The great Shun was greater still: he regarded goodness as something shared with others. He would give up his own way to follow others, and he delighted in learning from others in order to do good. From the time he plowed, sowed, made pottery and fished, until he became emperor, there was nothing he did not learn from others. To learn from others in order to do good is to do good together with others. So there is nothing greater for a gentleman than to do good together with others."

Mencius said, "Boyi would not serve a ruler who was not his proper ruler, and would not befriend anyone who was not his proper friend. He would not stand in the court of a wicked man, nor speak with a wicked man. To stand in the court of a wicked man or speak with a wicked man was to him like sitting in mud and soot in his court robes and cap. He carried his hatred of wickedness so far that if he was standing with a villager whose cap was not on straight, he would walk away without a backward glance, as if he would be defiled. So although some of the feudal lords came to him with courteous invitations, he would not accept. He would not accept because he disdained to go to them. Liuxia Hui was not ashamed to serve a corrupt ruler, nor did he think a small office beneath him. When he was promoted, he did not hide his worth, but always acted according to his Way. When he was dismissed and neglected, he did not complain; when he was in distress and poverty, he did not grieve. So he said, 'You are you and I am I. Even if you stand beside me stripped to the waist or stark naked, how can you defile me?' So he was quite at ease in the company of others without losing himself. If someone pulled him back to make him stay, he would stay. He stayed when pulled back because he disdained to leave." Mencius said, "Boyi was too narrow; Liuxia Hui was not respectful enough. A gentleman follows neither narrowness nor lack of respect."
